details:
**Black Death frame story (the brigata fleeing Florence)**
The frame narrative is set during the 1348 plague. A group called the "brigata," seven young women and three young men, meets at the Basilica of Santa Maria Novella and leaves Florence for countryside villas with gardens and fountains. There they tell ten stories a day for ten days, 100 tales in all, which gives the book its Greek-derived title meaning "ten days."

**Patient Griselda (Gualtieri, Marquis of Saluzzo)**
This is the final story of the collection (Day 10, Story 10), told by Dioneo. The nobleman Gualtieri marries the peasant Griselda and tests her obedience. He takes away their son and daughter, claims to have had them killed, and secretly sends them to Bologna. He then pretends to divorce her and sends her home, and later pretends to marry a twelve-year-old girl, who is actually their daughter. Griselda's unwavering patience is finally rewarded when he reveals the ruse.

**Dioneo**
Dioneo is the most mischievous member of the brigata and is often seen as a stand-in for Boccaccio himself. He is the only storyteller allowed to ignore the day's assigned theme, and he always tells the last tale of each day, including many of the bawdiest and wittiest stories and the closing Griselda tale.

**The Parable of the Three Rings (Melchizedek and Saladin)**
In this tale (Day 1, Story 3), told by Filomena, the sultan Saladin needs money and tries to trap the wealthy Jewish moneylender Melchizedek by asking which religion is true: Judaism, Christianity, or Islam. Melchizedek answers with a parable about a father who owns one precious ring. Unable to choose among his three sons, he has two identical copies made, so no one can tell which ring is the original. The parable inspired Gotthold Ephraim Lessing's Enlightenment play "Nathan the Wise."

**Federigo's falcon**
In a tale told by Fiammetta (Day 5, Story 9), the impoverished nobleman Federigo degli Alberighi has spent his fortune courting Monna Giovanna. When she unexpectedly visits him, he has nothing else to serve her, so he cooks his prized falcon, his last possession. She had actually come to ask for the falcon for her sick son. The son dies, and she later marries Federigo, moved by his generosity.

**Lisabetta's pot of basil**
In this tale told by Filomena (Day 4, Story 5), Lisabetta (Isabella) of Messina loves Lorenzo, but her three brothers secretly murder him. Guided by a dream, she digs up his body and cuts off his head. She buries the head in a pot of basil, which she waters with her tears. John Keats adapted the story as the poem "Isabella, or the Pot of Basil."

**Ser Ciappelletto (Cepparello)**
The book's first story, told by Panfilo, concerns Ser Cepparello of Prato, called Ciappelletto, a thoroughly wicked notary. While dying in Burgundy, he makes a completely false deathbed confession to a friar, even claiming to be a virgin. After his death he is venerated as a saint.

**Fiammetta, Pampinea, Filostrato, Panfilo, and Filomena**
These are major members of the brigata. The women are Pampinea, Fiammetta, Filomena, Emilia, Lauretta, Neifile, and Elissa, and the men are Panfilo, Filostrato, and Dioneo. Fiammetta is traditionally associated with Boccaccio's muse. Pampinea proposes fleeing the city, and Filostrato's name means "overcome by love."

**Kings and queens of the day**
Each day one member of the brigata is crowned king or queen and sets the theme for that day's stories. For example, Filostrato decrees that Day 4's tales concern loves with unhappy endings. Days 1 and 9 have no set theme. Boccaccio also interrupts the work with an authorial defense of his writing in the introduction to Day 4.

**Bridge of Geese**
In this tale (Day 9, Story 9), Giosefo goes to King Solomon for advice on handling his unruly, disobedient wife and is told to "go to the Bridge of Geese." There he sees a muleteer beating a stubborn mule across the bridge. Giosefo then applies the same violent tactic to his wife, who becomes obedient.

**Marguerite de Navarre's Heptameron**
The Decameron's format and title inspired the French queen Marguerite de Navarre's story collection "The Heptameron." It also uses a frame story of travelers telling tales, but she planned 100 stories and completed only 72 before her death.

**Peronella and the barrel**
In this tale (Day 7, Story 2), set in Naples, Peronella's husband returns home unexpectedly, so she hides her lover in a large barrel. She claims the man inside is a buyer inspecting the barrel. While the husband climbs in to scrape it clean, she and her lover resume their affair.

**Prince Galehaut (Principe Galeotto)**
This is the work's alternate title or subtitle. It refers to Galehaut, the go-between who brought together Lancelot and Guinevere in Arthurian romance. The name also echoes Dante's Francesca in "Inferno" Canto 5, who calls the book that led to her adultery a "Galeotto."

**Chaucer's "Clerk's Tale"**
In Geoffrey Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales," the Clerk tells the story of patient Griselda. Chaucer drew it from Boccaccio's final tale, largely through Petrarch's Latin translation of that story.

**Frate Alberto as the Archangel Gabriel**
In this tale (Day 4, Story 2), the hypocritical friar Alberto convinces a vain Venetian woman, Madonna Lisetta, that the Archangel Gabriel is in love with her. He then visits her bed disguised as the angel. When he is finally discovered, he escapes by leaping out her window into the canal.
